batchConsumer.before: Fifteen thousand messages, and a consumer that burned fifty million loop iterations per batch with a yield every five million so batches would overlap. Two minute fixture timeout, and it took 2:09 on this machine. The assurance was that a set of duplicates stayed empty.
batchConsumer.after: The sender chooses the identities and the assurance compares the delivered set with the sent set, so a duplicate and a loss each fail on their own sentence. The spin is a bounded thirty two yields, the timeout is thirty seconds, and two runs measured 24 s each.
batchConsumer.whyTheOldAssuranceWasHalf: A message the transport dropped never enters a duplicate set, so a loss passed the assertion and only appeared as the fixture timing out. Completion alone cannot see it either, because completion is raised once every identity has arrived; inactivity is the second way out and turns a loss into a failed sentence.
mutations: DUPLICATE -> 'the batch consumer saw a message identity more than once'
LOSS -> 'the delivered identities are not exactly the sent ones'

detail: Should_be_able_to_extract_timestamp and its process id sibling read the wall clock and accepted any timestamp within a minute while printing both for a human. They build a generator with a tick source the test chooses and compare the exact timestamp.

The first attempt configured the process wide NewId instead, which needs the shared generator reset for a tick provider to take effect. That reset moved the sequence every other test in the assembly shares and turned Should_be_using_the_correct_algorithm_for_sequential_guids red on a tick boundary. A local generator asserts the same thing and disturbs nothing.

The second attempt asserted that the process id changes a chosen substring of the identifier, which was a guess about where that value lands and was wrong. Two generators that differ only in the process provider are compared whole instead.

Should_be_completely_thread_safe_to_avoid_duplicates generated twenty million identifiers and printed how many duplicates it found, asserting nothing. It is bounded at 200000 and asserts that every identifier is distinct.

Should_generate_unique_identifiers_with_each_invocation compared each identifier only with the one before it, which a generator cycling through a small set would pass. It counts distinct identifiers now.

Should_be_fast_and_friendly measured throughput only and is removed rather than kept as a permanently excluded case. No NewId benchmark exists in the benchmark project to move it to, which is recorded rather than glossed over.
